title: Effects of fishery complementary photovoltaic power plant on near-surface meteorology and energy balance
abstract: Solar energy plays an essential role in achieving carbon goals and mitigating climate change. Therefore, solar power plants are rapidly developing in the renewable energy sector. However, many reports of solar power plants are on land, and extremely limited observational research has been conducted on the impacts of fishery complementary photovoltaic power plants (FPVs) on near-surface meteorology and surface energy. This study selected two adjacent eddy covariance observational towers at the fishery complementary photovoltaic power plant (FPV) in Yangzhong, Jiangsu Province, China, to explore this topic. The results indicated that the percent frequency of east wind (<4 m s−1) at 2 m decreased by 25.3% in the FPV site compared with the reference site. The FPV array has not an obvious heating effect on the ambient environment. The average air temperature difference in the two sites at 2 m and 10 m was 0.3 K and 0.1 K, respectively, during the heating period. The net radiation increased by 47.8 W m−2 in the two sites. The sensible heat increased by 7.9 W m−2 due to the heating effect. The latent heat in the two sites is contrary to the sensible heat (−13.0 W m−2). The difference in the water storage heat is 32.18 W m−2, which implies that the water absorbs higher heat in the FPV site than in the reference site. This work illustrated the importance of observational experiments to animate process-based understanding combined with FPV systems and provides a scientific basis for establishing FPV energy balance models based on observations that may be used to reveal the impact of utility-scale FPV deployment on climatic effects.

## 1. Introduction

Renewable energy plays a significant role in reaching the carbon-neutral goal [1] and slowing global warming. Solar energy is one of the most promising renewable energy sources because of its ubiquity and sustainability [2e6]. The capacity of utility-scale solar photovoltaic (PV) installations has exponentially increased [7]. Solar energy is expected to compose the majority of renewable energy production worldwide [8], and fulfill 20%e29% (32,700e133,000 GW) of global electricity demand by 2100 [9,10]. This transition should respond to the increase in the number of PV power plants and the deployment of PV modules. The energy

balance and the landscape in a local area were altered after the deployment of PV arrays by changing in shortwave and longwave radiation of absorption, storage, and release [11]. Thus, the proliferation of PV power plants has increased interest in the assessment of large-scale environmental effects [10,12e15]. Deployment of large-scale solar PVs has had a positive effect on greenhouse gas emissions (biogeochemical impacts), but an adverse effect on the local climate and hydrology because of the processes of site preparation and landscape modification, and solar radiation alteration. (biogeophysical impacts) [16].

Biogeophysical impacts are complicated because they relate to aspects of the lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, and biosphere on Earth's surface. The impact of utility-scale solar PV infrastructure on the local climate was driven by changes in landscape coverage and solar radiation. Masson et al. showed that roof PV has a heating effect in the summer [17]. Millstein et al. showed that the deployment of a PV array in the Mojave Desert of California has a heating effect [18]. farms in the Sahara Desert via a climate model with dynamic vegetation, in which the local temperature and precipitation were increased by more than two times, and this enhancement depends on the scale of the solar farm and is unique to the Sahara Desert [19]. These results demonstrate the heating effect of the deployment of large-scale solar PV systems on the local climate.

However, some reports have shown a cooling effect on the local temperature after installing solar PV [20e23]. An evaluation of solar PV on the environmental impact by modifying the surface albedo and emissivity is simplistic in the climate model. This phenomenon is because the climate model does not consider dynamic effects, because of the assumption that the deployment of solar PV alters the radiative fluxes. However, there is no consensus on the effect of solar PV on temperature.

The impact of solar PV on the local environment is not limited to temperature, and also affects the physical and chemical properties of the soil [10], precipitation and evaporation [24], biomass and species diversity [25], and wind patterns [26]. Nevertheless, the research sites are located on land, but land resources are scarce. The fishery PV power (FPV) plant is a new type of solar energy constructed on the water surface to avoid occupying land resources [27]. Additionally, the efficiency of solar energy is greater than that of land because of the cooling effect of the lake [5]. However, details of the surface energy balance of FPV solar on the lake and the latent impacts on the local environment are not clear. Thus, to understand the surface-atmosphere processes after installing the solar FPV, a sufficient amount of observational data is necessary to appraise the impact of solar FPV deployment on the local environment.

We used eddy covariance observation data from June 2020 to May 2021 to achieve the primary goal of revealing the process of energy balance modified by solar FPV on the lake and evaluate the impact of solar FPV arrays on local surface climate.

## 2. Site and methods

## 2.1. Site description

The research was undertaken at the 10 MW model base of a fishery complementary FPV in Tongwei Huantai. The model base of the fishery complementary FPV is located in northern Yangzhong, Jiangsu, China. This city has a mean annual temperature of 17.1[] C. The mean annual precipitation and the accumulated sunshine hours are 791.8 mm and 1792.2 h, respectively. The climate is mild, and the summer precipitation is high, with rain and heat over the same period.

The FPV plant is composed of four ponds of approximately 2.3e3.6 ha. The FPV arrays were deployed at the centre of the ponds with a water depth of approximately 2 m. Water depth is approximately 2.5 me3 m around the pond. A path approximately 3 m wide was embedded between each pond. The FPV panels were mounted on bracket bases on buried concrete columns. The gap between each column is 6 m. Each FPV module is 1.64 m by 0.99 m in dimension, and the portrait orientation of polycrystalline silicon FPV panels is south. The panels were installed at a tilt angle of 34.6[] from the horizontal, with the lower edge suited 1.6 m above the water surface. Two meteorological towers were deployed inside and outside the FPV plant (Fig. 1). The FPV site (Fig. 1a, blue pin) in the FPV array is located at 32[] 18[0] 9.00[00] N, 119[] 47[0] 33.45[00] E, with an elevation of 2 m above sea level. The reference site (REF; Fig. 1a, red pin, 32[] 18[0] 4.60[00] N, 119[] 47[0] 25.30[00] E, elevation 2 m above sea level) was erected outside the FPV plant approximately 250 m southwest of the FPV site.

## 2.2. Monitoring equipment & variables

Meteorological towers, each with a height of about 11 m, were deployed in the FPV and REF. The observation tower was equipped with a radiation system, an eddy covariance (EC) system, and three compact weather stations placed at different heights on the meteorological towers (Fig. 2).

A four-component net radiation sensor (CNR4, Kipp & Zonen) with a nonlinearity of less than 1% was mounted at 10 m on the tower in the FPV site. The height of CNR4 in the REF site is 2 m, which is lower than that of the FPV site without the impact of solar panels. The measured variables were the downward surface shortwave radiation (DSR, W$m[][2] ), upward surface shortwave radiation (USR, W$m[][2] ), downward surface longwave radiation (DLR, W$m[][2] ), upward surface longwave radiation (ULR, W$m[][2] ), and net radiation (Rn, W$m[][2] ).

Three compact weather stations (MaxiMet GMX600, Gill) were installed at heights of 2 m, 5 m, and 10 m on the tower, in the FPV site, in the REF, respectively. The accuracy and detailed parameters of the MaxiMet GMX600 are available on the datasheet on Table 1. The meteorological measurements were temperature ([] C), humidity (%), pressure (kPa), wind speed (m$s[][1] ), wind direction ([] ) and precipitation (mm).

Two EC systems (IRGASONeICeBB, Campbell Scientific, Inc.) were installed 4.5 and 3 m high in the FPV site and the REF, respectively. The heat flux and water vapour in the atmosphere were measured by a combination of an EC system, an open-path carbon dioxide and water vapour infrared gas analyser, and a three-dimensional sonic anemometer. The accuracy of the EC system was lower than ±8% cm$s[][1] for wind speed, and the frequency data were stored in a CR3000 data logger (Campbell Scientific, Inc.). The specifications of all the measuring instruments are listed in Table 1.

The water temperature was measured at three depths (0.05 m, 0.75 m, and 1.5 m) using a 109SS (Campbell Scientific, Inc.) temperature sensor. The measured instrument line was attached to a buoy and floated as the water level fluctuated to ensure that the position of each probe from the water surface was basically invariable.

The installation date of the radiation system, the EC system, and the water temperature system was Nov 11, 2019. However, data quality was poor because system maintenance did not occur on the appropriate date due to the coronavirus pandemic. Maintenance of the observational systems was delayed until June 3, 2020. Therefore, the data time range from June 7, 2020 to May 7, 2021. In addition, three compact weather stations were installed on December 6, 2020.

## 2.3. Data processing

The following procedures were performed to ensure the quality control of the raw data. For solar radiation, data exceeding the astronomical radiation and without simultaneous recording in the FPV site or the REF was excluded. The calibration of EC data was performed by EddyPro software, namely, filter and the diagnosis of 10 Hz data; coordinate rotation; and correct the time lag response, sonic virtual temperature, and WPL [28]. The raw observational data were calculated as 30 min averages by the CR3000 data logger to analyse of the results. The time system in this study was Beijing time.

## 3. Results and discussion

## 3.1. Wind and air temperature

Wind patterns of the FPV and REF sites are shown in Fig. 3. During the observational period, the wind regime of the FPV and REF sites was characterised by two prevailing winds, the east and southeast winds, respectively. The wind direction and wind speed were significantly different at various heights in the FPV site. The percent frequency of eastern wind at 2 m (44.9%) was reduced by 25.3% at 10 m (24.6%), and the east wind at 5 m was 27.5% in the FPV site. The percent frequency of the southeastern wind at 2 m, 5 m, and 10 m is 9.2%, 15.8%, and 16.6% in the FPV site, respectively. The east wind speed below 4 m s[][1] decreased from 27.5% at 2 m to 21.7% at 10 m in the FPV site. In the REF site (Fig. 3, second row), the pattern of wind speed is consistent with that of the FPV site (the wind pattern in the FPV site is consistent with turbulent drag, similar to the Ekman layer but at the micrometeorology scales), and with a decrease in height, the speed is attenuated between various heights. However, wind speed attenuation at the REF site is smaller than that of at the FPV site, and the wind direction at different heights was almost the same at both sites.

The prevailing wind is a relevant factor that influences wind pattern distribution at FPV sites. In addition, the installation height and orientation of the FPV affected the wind pattern. The upper edge of the PV panel facing south is 2.9 m from the water surface, obstructing the airflow in the north-south direction. Airflow below the height of the PV panel was blocked, which caused airflow direction to change and the speed to decrease. Wind directions in the REF site are more than the FPV site at 2 m, namely the northeast and northwest. The percent frequency of east and west winds was 4 m s[][1] at 2 m in the FPV site, which is less than that in the REF site.

Yin et al. [36] and Jiang et al. [37] have demonstrated that an PV array have a redirection effect on the wind. Our results also proved this effect.

The average air temperature at 2 m in the FPV site is 10.7[] C, which is higher than that in the REF site (10.5[] C; Fig. 4a). Specifically, from 06:00 to 14:00, the air temperature in the FPV is obviously higher than that in the REF site, indicating that the FPV array has a heating effect on the ambient temperature. This result is consistent with that of Broadbent et al. [38], but the underlying surface differed. Our findings show that the heat effect of the FPV array at ambient temperature is not related to the underlying surface. However, the degree of heating depends on the conditions of the underlying surface.

The daily maximum temperature and the daily maximum difference temperature between the FPV and REF sites were positively correlated (r 1⁄4 0.51, Fig. 4b). The magnitude of the heating effect varied from 0.05[] C to 2.39[] C during the study period, and the heating effect increased with an increase in the inside and outside FPV temperature. Barron-Gafford et al. [7] studied the effect of the PV heat island effect on local temperatures, and their results are consistent with those of this study. However, the heating effect was only explained by 26% (r[2] 1⁄4 0.26) through the daily maximum air temperature. Meteorological factors also affect the heating effect, such as the underlying surface, wind speed, cloud cover, and radiation. The heating effect on the air temperature affect the water temperature.

The near-surface air temperature profile to reveal the heating

The heating period (09:00e15:00) air temperature at 2 m and 10 m in the FPV site is 11.1[] C and 10.7[] C, and the REF site counterpart is 10.8[] C and 10.6[] C, respectively. The air temperature in the FPV site is 0.3 K and 0.1 K higher than that the REF site at 2 m and 10 m during the FPV array heating period, respectively. The temperature difference between the two sites are within the instrument errors. Based on Table 1, the uncertainty of the air temperature values is 0.3[] C, which is larger than the difference between the FPV and REF sites. Therefore, these results indicates that the FPV array has not an obvious heating effect on the near-surface air temperature. The reason for the phenomenon is that the daily maximum air temperature difference at 2 m is a positive relationship with the daily maximum air temperature at 2 m difference in two sites (Fig. 4b). Moreover, the deployment of the FPV array on the water surface increases the aerodynamic roughness for the FPV site, where the FPV modules enhance the vertical turbulent mixing by efficiently dissipating heat at the near-surface atmosphere. However, the degree of heating effect was attenuated with an increase in atmospheric height. Our results still show a heating effect at 10 m is not obvious. However, the heating effect in the daytime is inconsistent with the findings of Jiang et al. [37], Barron-Gafforf et al. [7], Chang et al. [39], Yang et al. [40], and Broadbent et al. [38]. The air temperature at 2 m and 10 m in the FPV site from 19:00 to 08:00, overnight, is 7.7[] C and 8.0[] C, and the REF site counterpart is 7.6[] C and 7.9[] C, respectively. The mechanism of the cooling effect is that the FPV modules impede the longwave radiative cooling of the underlying surface at night. Baron-Gafford et al. found that the PV array has a heating effect on the air temperature at midnight (3e4[] C) year round in southern Arizona [7]. Thus, the influence of the heating effect on the water temperature is discussed next to illuminate the feedback mechanism.

## 3.2. Water temperature

The FPV array has a heating effect on the surface water temperature (0 cm) during the observational period, with an average temperature increase of 0.11[] C (see Fig. 6). This difference may explain the higher ULR in the FPV site than in the REF site. The average water temperature at a depth of 50e150 cm in the FPV site is 1.83[] C lower than that in the REF site, which is caused by the physical-shaded function of the FPV panel. The temperature in the FPV at 150 cm is 4.87[] C lower than that in the REF site at the same depth, indicating that the shading function is obvious for the deeper water layer. In other words, the heating effect is limited to the transmission of the water layer. In addition, there is a difference between June and December for the degree of heating effect at a water depth of 150 cm. The magnitude of the heating effect depends on the difference (FPV-REF) of the surface water temperature at the two sites, with a difference in surface water temperature of 0.01[] C in June and 0.35[] C in December. ## 3.3. Radiation flux

According to the prior discussion, the impact of the FPV on the near-surface air temperature is asymmetric on a daily scale. Therefore, the radiation fluxes of the two sites were further analysed to determine whether there were differences in the radiation components at various seasonal scales (Fig. 7). The daily average DRn was higher in the FPV site than in the REF site over the entire period, with an average maximum Rn (FPV-REF) of 47.8 W m[][2] . The average maximum DRn in autumn is 31.2 W m[][2] greater than the winter (28.5 W m[][2] ), summer (17.7 W m[][2] ), and spring (7.4 W m[][2] ). The difference in Rn in various seasons was primarily because the USR was lower in the FPV site than in the REF site. The albedo decreased by 18.81% (from 0.101 to 0.082) after the deployment of the FPV array on the water surface in the FPV site compared with the REF site. Therefore, the shortwave radiation entering the atmosphere is decreased because of the reflection of

the underlying surface in the FPV plant, and the daily average USR in the FPV site during the whole period is 8.3 W m[][2] smaller than that of the REF site. The daily average USR difference corresponded to the diurnally averaged net radiation change of the two sites. To further describe the radiation force after installing the FPV array, we defined the radiation force ratio to display the degree of the net radiation change. Namely, the deficit Rn in two sites was divided by the Rn in the REF site, with a radiation force ratio of 45.9%.

With the long-wave radiation, the daily average ULR in the FPV site is 40.8 W m[][2] higher than the REF. The average maximum DULR in the daytime 89.3 W m[][2] , and the range is from 200.9 W m[][2] (spring) to 15.3 W m[][2] (autumn) during the observational period. In general, the shortwave and longwave radiation are consistent with the findings of another study [37,38,41]. The reasons for the difference in long waves at various timescales are complex. The difference in temperature caused a change in the longwave radiation in the two sites. In addition, the emission of the underlying surface affected the change in the ULR. Broadbent et al. [38] found that the upper surface FPV module is 0.11 lower than that of sandy soil, but the ULR in the FPV site is higher than that in

the REF site. The emission of the upper surface on lake (0.96) is approximately 0.04 higher than that of sandy soil (0.92). The installation of the deployment of the FPV array on the water surface has a higher emission (~0.02) than that on the free water surface, which may partially explain the increase in ULR during the daytime at the FPV site.

Jiang et al. [37] also found a pattern in desert areas where the ULR in FPV is 0.04 MJ m[][2] , which is slightly higher than that of the REF. Moreover, the distance between the radiometers and the upper FPV array affects the radiation components. Broadbent et al.’s results of the longwave is contrary to the Jiang et al.’s results, because the height of the radiometer is different between the PV site and the REF site (In Broadbent et al.’s study, the height of the radiometer in the PV site at 5.7 m and in the REF site at 2.8 m. In Jiang et al.’s study, the height of the radiometer in the PV site at 10 m and in the REF site at 3 m). In general, the FPV modules that absorbed shortwave radiation increased because of the decrease in surface albedo compared with the free water surface. Despite the larger Rn increase in the FPV site than in the REF site, the energy flux distribution at the two sites is ambiguous. Therefore, the partitioning of energy fluxes is explored to completely understand the drivers of the air temperature difference between the two sites.

## 3.4. Energy flux

The data of the sensible heat flux and latent heat flux were seriously missed in autumn and spring. Therefore, the energy flux was analysed, but not, in that period. The balance between water and heat on the surface is composed of H, LE, Rn, and DQ. The change in energy fluxes at the two sites is shown in Fig. 8aei. The H in the FPV site is 7.9 W m[][2] higher than that in the REF site for the whole time; the maximum DH (FPV-REF) is 39.1 W m[][2] at 12:00, again indicating that the FPV array has a heating effect on the air temperature. Simultaneously, the FPV site has a larger surface area and lower heat capacity than the REF site. Thus, the aerodynamic roughness is higher in the FPV site than in the REF site, resulting in heat dissipation in the near-surface air by turbulent diffusion, which heats the ambient air faster in the FPV site than in the REF site. However, the DLE in the two sites is contrary to DH, which is lower in the FPV site than in the REF site. The minimum DLE (FPVREF) is 98.1 W m[][2] at 9:00, and the average DLE is 13.0 W m[][2] , implying that the physical shaded function of FPV panel impedes the partial water evaporation. The DH in the two sites is 5.0 W m[][2] in winter, and 24.8 W m[][2] in summer. However, the change in DLE is not similar to that in DH in winter and summer for the FPV and REF sites. The average DLE is 43.3 W m[][2] in summer, and in winter, 16.1 W m[][2] , indicating that the degree of influence of the FPV panel's physical shaded effect on water evaporation is also related to the ambient temperature. In addition, the findings of Jiang et al. showed that the difference in DH increased from the PV site to the REF site due to the augmentation of the heat transference, in which DLE decreased because of the attenuation of the wind speed from the PV site to the REF site [37].

The positive or negative values of DQ represent the absorption of heat or release heat. The difference (FPVeREF) of DQ in the two sites was 32.18 W m[][2] during the observational period, which implies that the water in the FPV site absorbs higher heat relative to the REF site. This result indicated the FPV panels have a heating effect on water. The maximum difference of DQ (FPV - REF) is 185.8 W m[][2] at 19:00, and the minimum difference of DQ

is 127.14 W m[][2] at 11:00. For the FPV site, the maximum DQ is 65.2 W m[][2] at 13:00, but the maximum DQ in the REF site at 11:00 is 153.0 W m[][2] . The peak DQ in the FPV site is lower than that in the REF site because the degree of the tilted FPV panel that resists the downward shortwave solar radiation is higher than the heating effect on water. Additionally, there is a lag time for water to absorb heat from ambient to peak in the two sites. In addition, the difference in DQ showed contrary characteristics between summer and winter in both sites. Namely, the difference in DQ in summer and winter is 6.1 W m[][2] and 57.0 W m[][2] , respectively. The results indicated that water releases more heat in the FPV site than in the REF site in summer and vice versa in winter.

The period of robust power generation of the FPV power plant was selected to analyse the energy balance closure. We attempted to reveal the impact of the PV power generation process on the degree of energy balance closure by comparing the EBR inside and outside the FPV power plant. The EBRs at different time spans are shown in Table 2. During the entire study period, the average EBR of the PV site was 0.05 higher than that of the REF site. In summer, the EBR difference between the PV and REF sites can reach 0.13. However, the degree of the EBR difference in winter was 0.07, which is smaller than that in summer. This difference is because the air temperature is higher in summer than in winter, the solar panels have the largest heating effect on the air temperature in summer, and the degree of change in lake sensible heat and latent heat flux is stronger than that in winter. Additionally, the depth of the lake is smaller, and the vertical water mixture is stronger, which causes a high-frequency change in the heat storage of the lake with the heating effect. In addition, the EBR in FPV power plants is lower than that in similar lakes because the solar panels convert approximately 15% of the short radiation into electricity. Therefore, the EBR in the FPV site was smaller than that in the REF site during the entire study period.

## 4. Conclusion

This study presents measurements of microclimate factors, radiation flux, and energy balance above the fishery complementary PV power plant. We found that the FPV array has not an obvious heating effect on the ambient environment during the entire observational period. For the microclimate condition, the FPV array affected the wind speed and direction. With the wind flowing through the FPV array, the tilted FPV panel resists the wind speed and changes the flowing air direction in the FPV site relative to the REF site to redistribute the wind pattern. Most notably, the percent frequency of east wind (4 m s[][1] ) in the FPV site at 2 m decreased by 25.3% compared with the REF site because the FPV panel is approximately 0.2 m higher than the installation of the temperature sensor. The difference in the water storage heat is 32.18 W m[][2] , which implies that the water absorbs more heat in the FPV site more than in the REF site. Therefore, this result indicates the heating effect of FPV array.

The literature has only studied the impact of FPV plants on the environment in a local area in Yangzhong. The impact of FPV plants on water at the regional and global scales should combine climate numerical models to further investigate the mechanisms of climate and environment feedback effects. Moreover, the fishery complementary PV system is fix-mounted panels in this study. Floating PVs have attracted the interest of scholars due to their advantages over other panel types, such as the reduction of evaporation loss. However, difference in the impact of fix-mounted PVs and floating PVs on solar radiation and energy balance is unclear because of the difference in the covering water area or albedo, and the effects of different PV systems will be evaluated in further research.
